questions.enonce_markdown:
Explain with examples, the following systems of taxation:

(i) Proportional tax. (4 marks)

(ii) Progressive tax. (4 marks)

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Proportional tax (4 marks)**

A **proportional tax** takes the **same percentage (rate) of income** from everybody, whatever the level of income. The rate stays constant, so the amount paid rises in proportion to income.

*Example (hypothetical, 10% tax):*

| Income (FCFA) | Tax at 10% (FCFA) | Rate |
|---|---|---|
| 100 000 | 10 000 | 10% |
| 500 000 | 50 000 | 10% |

A person who earns five times more pays five times more tax, but at the **same rate**. A flat rate sales tax or company tax at a fixed percentage is an example.

**(ii) Progressive tax (4 marks)**

A **progressive tax** takes a **higher percentage of income as income increases**: the rate rises with income, so the rich pay a larger proportion of their income than the poor. It is based on the **ability to pay** and reduces inequality.

*Example (hypothetical rates):*

| Income (FCFA) | Rate | Tax (FCFA) |
|---|---|---|
| 100 000 | 5% | 5 000 |
| 300 000 | 10% | 30 000 |
| 600 000 | 20% | 120 000 |

The person earning 600 000 FCFA pays 20% of income, four times the rate of the person earning 100 000 FCFA. Personal income tax is usually progressive.

questions.enonce_markdown:
State and explain four ways by which the Cameroon government spends its revenue.

(12 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The government of Cameroon obtains **revenue** from taxes, oil and other resources, fees and borrowing, and spends it on the following items.

**1. Recurrent expenditure (salaries and running costs).** The government pays the **salaries of civil servants** (teachers, doctors, police, soldiers) and the costs of running ministries, schools and hospitals, such as electricity, water, stationery and the maintenance of buildings. It is spent every year and forms a large part of the budget.

**2. Capital expenditure (investment in infrastructure).** The government spends on **building and repairing roads, bridges, ports, schools, hospitals, dams and electricity and water systems**. This spending **promotes economic growth** and development, because infrastructure lowers the costs of firms and attracts investors.

**3. Social services (education, health and social welfare).** The government spends on **free or subsidised education and health care**, scholarships, pensions and help to vulnerable people. This improves the **standard of living** and the quality of the labour force.

**4. Public debt service.** The government must **repay loans and pay the interest** on domestic and foreign borrowing. This reduces the amount left for development spending.

**Other ways:** **defence and security** (army, police), **subsidies and transfer payments** (for example support to farmers or fuel), contributions to international organisations and the running of embassies.

**Conclusion.** The government spends its revenue on running the State, building infrastructure, providing social services and repaying debts, in order to promote growth and the welfare of the people.
